core: Performance assessment: why some constructs (writing, argument, design, investigation, performance) require the student to produce the performance rather than select a response
Authentic assessment as a design goal about the task's resemblance to real practice, and why authenticity is not by itself evidence of validity
Rubric anatomy: criteria, performance levels, and performance level descriptors
The distinction between a rubric, a checklist, and a rating scale
Analytic, holistic, and single-point rubrics and the purposes each fits
Writing descriptors that describe quality rather than counting features or rating effort; the 'few / some / many errors' failure mode
Criteria that describe learning versus criteria that restate assignment directions
Rater training, calibration, moderation and monitoring as the machinery that makes judged scores usable
Common rater effects: severity/leniency, centrality, halo, and inconsistency (misfit)
Task sampling variability as the dominant source of measurement error in performance assessment
The tension between rubric specificity and construct validity: over-specified rubrics can convert a complex performance into a compliance checklist
Using rubrics with students before performance, including self-assessment and peer assessment, and the honest state of the evidence
supporting: Generalizability theory as the framing that lets tasks, raters, occasions and methods be treated as sampling facets (named, not taught)
Operational monitoring practice in a large federal assessment programme (NAEP backreading, calibration sets, trend scoring)
Publication bias as a reason to read the rubric-effects literature cautiously
outOfScope: Reliability and validity theory, coefficient choice, kappa, and the AERA/APA/NCME Standards framework, which belong to education:assessment:reliability-and-validity-in-assessment
The formative versus summative distinction as a topic, owned by education:assessment:formative-versus-summative-assessment
Grading policy, weighting, points-to-letter conversion and standards-based grading systems
Writing learning objectives and Bloom-style verb selection, owned by education:teaching-and-instruction:writing-learning-objectives
Automated essay scoring and machine scoring of constructed response
Accountability policy, test-based teacher evaluation, and large-scale assessment law

claims.claim: Performance assessment examines student performance on intellectual tasks directly, whereas conventional selected-response testing relies on indirect proxy items from which performance is inferred; Wiggins argued that if the valued outcome is problem-posing, experimental investigation, discussion, document-based inquiry or sustained revision of writing, the assessment should be built out of those challenges.

Wiggins framed authenticity as a property of assessment design - tasks that mirror the priorities and ill-structured challenges of real intellectual work, with challenges known in advance so students can rehearse - and argued that authentic assessment achieves validity and reliability by standardising the criteria used to score varied products rather than by standardising items. Authenticity is therefore an argument about task design; it is not itself evidence that score interpretations are valid.

A rubric has two parts: criteria stating what to look for in the work, and performance level descriptions stating what those criteria look like in work of varying quality. The presence of both is what distinguishes a rubric from a checklist (dichotomous has/does-not-have decisions) and from a rating scale (a numeric, evaluative or frequency scale that does not describe the performance).

Analytic rubrics judge each criterion separately and are better suited to feedback; holistic rubrics require a single judgment across all criteria simultaneously and are quicker, so they suit grading situations where students will not act on the feedback.

A single-point rubric states only the proficient level for each criterion, leaving an open column on each side for evidence of shortfall and evidence of work that exceeds the target; Fluckiger presented it as a tool for student goal-setting and self-assessment.

Performance level descriptions should describe the quality of the work rather than count occurrences of features or use bare evaluative labels. In Brookhart's review of 51 rubrics from 46 higher-education studies, 7 rubrics used rating-scale language or relied on counting occurrences instead of describing quality; she judged such tools more useful for grading than for learning.

Criteria that restate the directions for an assignment rather than describe learning - Brookhart's example contrasts 'has three sources' with 'uses a variety of relevant, credible sources' - misdirect student effort and mis-measure learning.

Across the 46 higher-education studies Brookhart reviewed, 29 of 51 rubrics (about 57 percent) were analytic descriptive rubrics, and only 56 percent of the studies reported using the rubric with students at all.

Jonsson and Svingby's review of 75 empirical studies concluded that rubrics can improve the reliability of scoring performance assessments, especially analytic, topic-specific rubrics accompanied by exemplars and/or rater training, but that rubrics do not by themselves produce valid judgments of performance.

Panadero and Jonsson's review of 21 studies of formative rubric use found that rubrics may improve performance indirectly by increasing transparency, reducing anxiety, aiding feedback, improving self-efficacy and supporting self-regulation; effects appear to depend on implementation, and in studies where rubrics were simply handed out without training there were typically no significant effects on performance.

Reported findings on rubric effects should be read cautiously: in Brookhart's review, every study reported positive outcomes for rubric use and no relationship was found between rubric type or quality and study results, which she attributed in part to possible publication bias.

In Shavelson, Gao and Baxter's generalizability studies of elementary mathematics and science performance assessments, variance components for rater, person-by-rater and task-by-rater were zero or negligible, so one well-trained rater could be sufficient; task-sampling variability was the major source of measurement error.

With one rater and one task, relative generalizability coefficients in that work were 0.15, 0.21 and 0.32 for the Science, Math and California Assessment Program data sets; reaching a relative generalizability coefficient near .80 was estimated to require about 23 tasks for the Science study, 15 for the Math study and 8 for the CAP study.

Rater effects are systematic tendencies in raters rather than in students: severity/leniency (scoring consistently lower or higher than the performance warrants) and centrality (restricting ratings to the middle categories of the scale) are two of the standard categories, alongside rater misfit, which is inconsistent, idiosyncratic scoring.

In Wind's simulation study, when as few as about 10 percent of raters exhibited a rater effect there were substantial changes in student classifications, and rater severity produced larger impacts on achievement estimates and classification consistency than centrality or misfit.

The halo effect is a rater's tendency to let performance in general, or on one trait, influence the ratings given on other traits, producing intercategory correlations higher than reality; because it produces repetitious ratings it inflates reliability estimates rather than lowering them. Central tendency is a special case of restriction of range in which a rater avoids both extremes of the scale and rates nearly everyone as average.

Rater errors are a source of construct-irrelevant variance and are detectable in real programmes: a many-facet Rasch analysis of a clinical skills assessment of 173 fourth-year medical students rated by standardized patients found statistically significant differences in rater severity and inconsistency in four raters, while halo and restriction of range were not detected.

Operational scoring programmes control rater consistency with training, calibration sets and continuous monitoring; NAEP supervisors backread a target of at least five percent of each scorer's daily work to check that the scoring guide is being applied correctly, and trainers use calibration sets to prevent teams from drifting away from the scoring standard.

Wiggins anticipated public doubt about judged scores and pointed to established programmes - New York Regents essays, Advanced Placement open-ended and portfolio tasks, state writing assessments and NAEP - that obtain adequate reliability through reader training, model papers used as exemplars, blind reading, and audit and oversight procedures.

There is a real tension between specificity and construct validity: topic-specific rubrics tend to raise scoring reliability, while general rubrics apply to a family of tasks and can be shared with students for learning; task-specific rubrics specify the facts, concepts or procedures a response should contain and cannot be shared in advance without giving away the answer.

positions: Panadero and Jonsson (2013) conclude rubrics may improve performance and self-regulation through several mediating mechanisms, with effects moderated by implementation length, educational level and accompanying metacognitive activity.

Jonsson and Svingby (2007) reported that no conclusion about student improvement could be drawn from the earlier literature because results were mixed, and studies in which rubrics were handed out without training typically showed no significant effect.
Brookhart (2018) found every reviewed study reported positive outcomes and no relationship between rubric type or quality and results, and raised publication bias as a likely explanation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that rubrics can improve scoring consistency and are associated with improved student performance, that the effect appears to depend on how the rubric is used with students rather than on the document itself, and that the published literature skews positive. No effect size is asserted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is rater disagreement or task sampling the bigger threat to performance-assessment scores?
positions: Historically the technical worry was inter-rater reliability.
Shavelson, Gao and Baxter (1993) found rater-sampling variability negligible once raters were trained, with task sampling the dominant error source.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches rater control as necessary but solvable, and task sampling as the harder, under-appreciated threat. The generalizability figures are attributed to elementary mathematics and science tasks in that study rather than presented as universal constants.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does making a rubric more specific make the assessment better?
positions: Jonsson and Svingby (2007): topic-specific analytic rubrics with exemplars and rater training improve scoring reliability.

Brookhart (2018) and the critiques she summarises (Sadler, Torrance, Nordrum et al.): over-specified or directions-based criteria narrow what students understand the learning to be and can mis-measure it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a genuine trade-off rather than a settled rule: specificity buys agreement but can shift the construct from the performance to compliance with the specification.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive claims about rubrics or performance assessment at all; its body text was subject-agnostic boilerplate ('a foundational concept in Education', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') that could have been written about any topic.
The draft's three quick-check questions tested nothing about rubrics, performance tasks, criteria, descriptors, raters or task sampling.
The draft carried an empty sources array while presenting definitional claims.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generated boilerplate with researched content on performance assessment, rubric anatomy and the measurement problems specific to rated performances.

Corrected the implicit framing that a rubric is a grading form: the reviewed literature distinguishes rubrics from rating scales and point schemes, and only about half the reviewed studies used the rubric with students.
Added the task-sampling threat, which is the single most consequential technical fact about performance assessment and was absent from the draft.
Added the honest caveat that 'authentic' describes task design and is not itself validity evidence.
Added a publication-bias caution rather than reporting rubric benefits as settled.
rightsIssues: Brookhart (2018) is CC BY 4.0 and could be adapted with attribution; even so, all prose in this lesson is original synthesis and no passage was reproduced.
The Wiggins ERIC Digest states that permission is granted to copy and distribute it; it was still summarised in original wording.
Panadero and Jonsson (2013) was read as an author-hosted preprint whose notice states it may not be uploaded to an open repository; it is treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and nothing was reproduced.

Jonsson and Svingby (2007) was verified from the ERIC catalogue record and abstract only; the full text sits behind an Elsevier paywall, so claims attributed to it are limited to what the abstract states.

Fluckiger (2010) full text returned HTTP 403 from the institutional repository; only the repository record and abstract were verified, so it is cited only for the purpose and existence of the single-point rubric, with the column structure supported independently by the NC State DELTA page.
The CRESST technical report is Copyright 1993 The Regents of the University of California; figures are cited and attributed, no passage reproduced.
NCES NAEP technical documentation pages carry no explicit licence statement and are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY.

sourceRecords.title: Sampling Variability of Performance Assessments (CSE Technical Report 361)
sourceRecords.provider: Richard J. Shavelson, Xiaohong Gao and Gail P. Baxter, University of California, Santa Barbara / National Center for Research on Evaluation, Standards, and Student Testing (CRESST), UCLA
sourceRecords.notes: Full 30-page technical report downloaded and text-extracted. Supports the sampling framing of a performance score (tasks, occasions, raters, methods as facets), the finding that rater, person-by-rater and task-by-rater variance components were zero or negligible so one well-trained rater may suffice, the finding that task-sampling variability was the major source of measurement error, the single-rater single-task relative G coefficients of 0.15, 0.21 and 0.32 for the Science, Math and CAP data sets, and the estimates of about 23, 15 and 8 tasks respectively to reach a relative G coefficient near .80. Copyright 1993 The Regents of the University of California; a version was published in the Journal of Educational Measurement. No passage reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Appropriate Criteria: Key to Effective Rubrics
sourceRecords.provider: Susan M. Brookhart, Duquesne University; Frontiers in Education 3:22
sourceRecords.license: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution License), stated in the article
sourceRecords.notes: Full 12-page article downloaded and text-extracted. Supports the two-part definition of a rubric (criteria plus performance level descriptions), the separation of rubrics from checklists and rating scales, the general-versus-task-specific distinction, the analytic-versus-holistic purposes, the 'has three sources' versus 'uses a variety of relevant, credible sources' example of directions-as-criteria, and the review counts: 46 studies yielding 51 rubrics, 29 of 51 analytic descriptive, 7 of 51 using rating-scale language or counting occurrences, only 56 percent of studies reporting rubric use with students, no relationship between rubric type or quality and study results, and the author's own publication-bias caution. No passage reproduced despite the permissive licence.

sourceRecords.title: The Use of Scoring Rubrics for Formative Assessment Purposes Revisited: A Review (EJ999454)
sourceRecords.provider: Ernesto Panadero and Anders Jonsson; Educational Research Review 9, 129-144; ERIC catalogue record
sourceRecords.notes: The authors' own accepted-manuscript preprint (hosted at ernestopanadero.es) was read in full for the discussion section; its notice permits personal use only and forbids upload to an open repository, so the ERIC record is given as the citation URL and nothing is reproduced. Supports the count of 21 reviewed studies, the five proposed mediating mechanisms (transparency, reduced anxiety, aided feedback, self-efficacy, self-regulation), the moderating role of implementation length, educational level and accompanying metacognitive activity, and the observation that studies handing rubrics to students without training typically found no significant performance effect.

sourceRecords.title: The Use of Scoring Rubrics: Reliability, Validity and Educational Consequences (EJ796733)
sourceRecords.provider: Anders Jonsson and Gunilla Svingby; Educational Research Review 2(2), 130-144; ERIC catalogue record
sourceRecords.notes: Only the ERIC catalogue record and abstract were accessible; the full text is behind an Elsevier paywall. Claims attributed here are limited to the abstract's three conclusions: that reliable scoring of performance assessments can be enhanced by rubrics, especially analytic, topic-specific rubrics complemented by exemplars and/or rater training; that rubrics do not facilitate valid judgment per se; and that rubrics have potential to promote learning by making expectations and criteria explicit. The review covered 75 empirical studies.

sourceRecords.title: NAEP Technical Documentation: Backreading
sourceRecords.provider: National Center for Education Statistics, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the definition of backreading as a supervisor reviewing already-scored responses to check that the scoring guide is being applied correctly, the target of backreading at least five percent of all scorer work on a daily basis, and the practice of resuming group training when backreading reveals errors common to several scorers.

sourceRecords.title: NAEP Technical Documentation: Scoring Monitoring
sourceRecords.provider: National Center for Education Statistics, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the description of ongoing scorer monitoring in a large operational programme: trainers responsible for keeping team interrater agreement high, calibration sets used to stop teams drifting from the scoring standard, within-year interrater agreement checks, and trend scoring used to compare agreement across years.

sourceRecords.title: Examining the Impacts of Rater Effects in Performance Assessments
sourceRecords.provider: Stefanie A. Wind, University of Alabama; Applied Psychological Measurement 43(2), 159-171; open-access copy via PubMed Central (PMC6376535)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the definitions of rater severity/leniency, centrality and misfit as systematic rater effects, and the simulation findings that substantial changes in student classifications occurred when about 10 percent of raters displayed an effect and that severity produced larger impacts on achievement estimates and classification consistency than centrality or misfit. Copyright the author(s) 2018; no passage reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: How Good Are Our Raters? Rater Errors in Clinical Skills Assessment (ED494160)
sourceRecords.provider: Cherdsak Iramaneerat and Rachel Yudkowsky, University of Illinois at Chicago; conference paper archived in ERIC, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Full 22-page ERIC full-text paper downloaded and text-extracted. Supports the framing of rater effects as construct-irrelevant variance arising from rater behaviour rather than ratee performance, the definition and history of the halo effect (Wells 1907, Thorndike, Newcomb) as one trait or a general impression influencing ratings of other traits and producing intercategory correlations higher than reality, the observation that halo inflates rather than lowers reliability estimates, and the definition of central tendency as a special case of restriction of range. Also supports the study finding that in a clinical skills assessment of 173 fourth-year medical students rated by standardized patients, severity/leniency differences and inconsistency in four raters were detected while halo and restriction of range were not. Conference paper, not journal peer review; used for standard definitions and one illustrative result.
